# AI as Consumption Enhancer, Not Writing Tool

## The Verboten Rule

Wang has a rule about AI in his own writing process. The rule is one word.

*Verboten.*[^1]

He says this, on the podcast, with the specific awareness that the word is a strong one. *I will try as much as possible and perhaps even declare it verboten not to let AI get into my writing. I don't want it prompted to have any sentences that I could actually just use. I want the sentences to come from within myself.*[^1]

This is interesting because Wang is not an AI skeptic. He is, by his own account, *using AI all the time.*[^1] He uses it for restaurant recommendations. He uses it to talk about music. He uses it to think through novels he has just read. He uses it for art, for conversations about culture, for the kind of curiosity-driven exploration that used to require either a knowledgeable friend or a great library or both. He calls it a *super tool.*[^1] The praise is sincere.

But the moment AI approaches his writing, the door closes. Not for ideological reasons. Not because Wang thinks the model can't produce serviceable prose. The opposite, in fact — Wang's complaint about AI prose is that the sentences are *generally super flat*, and his concern is precisely that he might *use* them.[^1] The verboten is a defense against the temptation. He knows he could prompt the model to produce a sentence that would be good enough to drop into his manuscript, and he is closing that door before he opens it.

The rule is built around a specific theory of what writing is and what would be lost if AI got into it. Understanding the theory is the work of this page.

## The Theory: Sentences as Self

When Wang says *I want the sentences to come from within myself*, the phrase is doing more work than it sounds like.[^1] He is not making a Romantic claim about authentic self-expression. He is making a much more specific claim: *the sentences in my writing are how my mind organizes itself, and if those sentences are produced by a system that is not my mind, the writing stops being a record of my mind and becomes a record of something else.*

This is closer to the cognitive-neuroscience claim that thinking happens partly *in the act of writing* than to any aesthetic preference. The writer who outsources sentence-construction is outsourcing the cognition that the sentence-construction would have produced. They get the sentence, but they don't get the thought the sentence-construction would have surfaced — the half-formed insight that becomes visible only when the writer has to find the words for it, the constraint that produces a sharper formulation when the obvious one fails. None of this happens when the model produces the sentence. The output looks like writing; the underlying thinking has not occurred.

For Wang specifically, who has built his analytical voice on *texture* and *zoom in/out across scales* and *sentence as structural anchor for an entire essay*, the loss would be catastrophic. Wang's voice is constituted by the cognition that produces his sentences. If the model were producing the sentences, Wang would still be the author of the byline but not the author of the voice. The voice would degrade by exactly the amount that the model's contribution increased. Over time, with continued use, the voice would converge toward what models produce when prompted to write like Dan Wang — which is not what Dan Wang produces when Dan Wang writes.

The verboten is not a limit on AI capability. It is a defense of the cognition that the writing is supposed to be *of*.

## The Permitted Side: AI as Consumption Engine

The defense of writing happens alongside an enthusiastic embrace of AI in another domain. Wang's framing is that AI is *primarily a form to enhance my consumption.*[^1] The phrase is more careful than it first appears — he does not say "consumption" loosely; he is staking a claim about the kind of activity AI is structurally well-suited to.

What does *enhanced consumption* look like in practice?

**Music.** Wang knows little about music theory. He listens to Mozart, Beethoven, Mahler with affection but without the technical vocabulary to describe what he's hearing. With AI, he can ask: *what should I listen to in this string quartet, what is happening in the second movement, why does this passage feel different from the rest of the piece?* The AI provides a musicological gloss that Wang could not have produced himself and that, in his Ottawa childhood, would have required either a music professor or hours in a music library. *In terms of a counterfactual of what I couldn't get before to what I can get now, it might be the place with the biggest delta in all of the AI world.*[^1]

**Novels.** Wang reread Stendhal's *The Red and the Black* in the summer of 2025. After finishing, he interrogated the AI about the novel — what literary scholars and critics have said, which interpretive frames have been developed, what the consensus and contested readings are. His own experience of the novel had been ecstatic and personal, *necessarily individual*. The AI conversation was not a substitute for that experience; it was a *layer added on top of it*, providing the critical apparatus that allows the reader to think about what they have just read.[^1]

**Restaurants and clothing.** Pedestrian, in the literal sense — Wang asks AI for a noodle shop in a neighborhood, for a piece of clothing he is interested in. The AI is functioning as a knowledgeable friend who has read everything and remembers everything, available at any time of day.

**Music and art conversation generally.** *I think the AI is really really good for thinking through a lot of these different sort of things.*[^1]

The pattern across these uses is that the AI is providing *structured access to expert knowledge that the user is not themselves expert in*, oriented toward the user's existing experience rather than producing new artifacts. Wang has the experience of reading Stendhal; the AI provides the critical apparatus. Wang has the experience of hearing Mozart; the AI provides the musicological gloss. Wang has eaten somewhere; the AI suggests a similar place. The AI is a layer on top of Wang's life, not a substitute for it.

This is what *enhanced consumption* means. The user keeps doing the experiencing — the reading, the listening, the eating, the looking — and the AI enriches the layer of understanding that wraps around the experiencing.

## Why the Boundary Holds

The boundary between *enhanced consumption* and *substituted production* is the operative line in Wang's framework. Why does it hold?

The boundary holds because the two activities have different relationships to the user's cognition.

*Consumption* is downstream of the user's experience. The user has read the novel. The user has eaten at the restaurant. The user has heard the piece. The AI's contribution is critical commentary, comparative context, expert framing — all of which are *additive* to the user's already-existing cognitive engagement with the object. The user is enriched by the AI's contribution, but the user's underlying cognitive activity is unchanged.

*Production* is the cognitive activity itself. The user is generating sentences, arguments, structural choices. If the AI substitutes for the user's sentence-generation, the user has not done the thinking the sentences encode. The output exists, but the thinking does not. The user is impoverished, even if the output is fine.

The same AI tool is acting on opposite sides of the boundary in the two cases. In consumption, the AI augments cognition. In production, the AI replaces it. Wang is not making an across-the-board claim about AI; he is making a *boundary* claim. Use it on this side. Don't let it cross to the other side.

The boundary may be hard to maintain in practice because the same interface is available for both. ChatGPT will discuss Stendhal with you and ChatGPT will write you a passage about Stendhal in the style of a particular essayist. The first is consumption-enhancement; the second is production-substitution. The user has to *decide* which mode they're in, and the decision has to be sustained against the constant temptation to slip from one to the other. Wang's verboten is the discipline that holds the boundary against the slippage.

## The Live-Before-AI Argument

Wang adds a separate but related argument about *when* AI should enter a person's life. The argument is generational and structural.

He frames it through Tyler Cowen's experience. The internet *dropped into Tyler's lap about halfway through his life. He had already gotten his PhD. He had already taught at UC Irvine and George Mason before the internet became a really big thing in the late 90s.*[^1] Tyler arrived at the internet with a fully developed cognitive apparatus — research skills, writing discipline, intellectual networks, the habit of going to libraries. The internet *turbocharged* what Tyler already was; it did not replace the cognitive infrastructure he had built before it arrived.

Wang applies the same logic to himself and AI. Wang is 33. ChatGPT *blew up* when he was 30. He has *lived half my life without AI*, and he proposes to *let the super tool take over my life in the second half.*[^1] The structure matters. The first half built the cognitive infrastructure — *go to the library, check out the databases on FRED, do some spreadsheets, do some PowerPoint presentations, learn a lot of these basic skills, learn how to read*[^1] — and now the AI arrives as a multiplier on top of those skills.

The contrast is with Stanford undergrads in 2026. Wang sees them at the Hoover Institution library, *using ChatGPT to check through everything that they want to do and then once they're done with that they're watching some TikTok short videos.*[^1] His judgment is gentle but firm: *that just doesn't feel like that's the very best form of learning to me.* The undergrads are skipping the cognitive infrastructure layer that Tyler and Wang built before AI arrived. They are letting the multiplier operate without the underlying skills it is supposed to multiply, and the result will be people who can deploy AI fluently without having developed the cognition the AI is supposed to amplify.

This is not a claim that the undergrads will fail. It is a claim that they are missing something. The experience of *not knowing the answer*, *having to find it*, *building the muscle of finding it*, is the foundation that makes the AI multiplier produce more rather than substitute for. Skip the foundation, and the multiplier multiplies less.

## What This Means for Practice

The framework converts cleanly into a set of practical heuristics for the writer or analyst working with AI.

**Heuristic 1: Identify which side of the consumption-production boundary you are on right now.**

When you sit down at the keyboard, the first question is whether this is a consumption session or a production session. *Asking AI about a topic you want to understand* is consumption. *Generating a paragraph for a piece you are writing* is production. The two activities should happen in different sessions, ideally on different days, because the cognitive mode required for each is different and the slippage between them is dangerous.

**Heuristic 2: Use AI freely on the consumption side.**

The conservative posture toward AI is wrong on the consumption side. AI conversation about novels, music, art, history, restaurants, clothing, philosophy, science is genuinely enriching, and the user who refuses to use AI on the consumption side is leaving signal on the table. Wang's enthusiasm here is not exaggerated — the music-and-novel use case really is one of the highest-leverage applications of current AI for non-specialists.

**Heuristic 3: Maintain the verboten on the production side.**

The user who wants to develop a distinctive voice, to do the cognitive work that writing is *for*, to produce sentences that record their own mind's organization — that user has to keep AI out of the sentence-generation step. Drafting, revising, structural decisions, sentence rhythm, word choice — all of this has to be human, all the way through, every time. Some users will choose to relax this constraint for utilitarian writing where voice is not the point (corporate emails, technical documentation, press releases). For voice-bearing writing, the verboten holds.

**Heuristic 4: For new users, build the cognitive infrastructure first.**

If you are young or newly engaging with serious cognitive work, the order matters. Spend two or three years using libraries, databases, spreadsheets, paper notes, longhand drafting, and other pre-AI cognitive tools before letting AI become your default. The infrastructure built in the pre-AI phase becomes the foundation that AI later multiplies. Skip the foundation and the multiplier multiplies a smaller thing.

## Tensions

The framing has a clear tension with the broader vault apparatus on AI-as-creative-collaborator. The existing pages — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/taste-judgment-labor-framework|Taste, Judgment, Labor Framework]], [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/vast-voice-print-method|VAST Voice Print Method]], [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/ai-first-design-workflow|AI First Design Workflow]] — treat AI as a legitimate participant in the creative-production process, with the human providing taste, judgment, and aesthetic constraints while delegating substantial labor to the model. Wang's framework rejects this as a category error for *voice-bearing writing*: the labor of sentence-generation is constitutive of voice, and delegating it impoverishes the writer even when the output is fine.

The tension is not a contradiction. The two frameworks may both be correct for different writing forms. The taste-judgment-labor framework may apply well to writing where voice is not the central currency — corporate copy, marketing, technical documentation. Wang's framework may apply specifically to writing where voice *is* the central currency — essay, analysis, literary nonfiction, anywhere the writer's distinctive cognition is what readers are buying. The vault should hold both as live frames and apply them to different cases. The collision between them is a meaningful one and should be filed as such.

The deeper tension is over what *production* means. The taste-judgment-labor framework treats production as factorable into components, some of which can be delegated. Wang's framework treats production as a unitary cognitive activity that loses something specific when it is factored. Whether production is in fact factorable in the way the labor framework assumes is the live empirical question. The honest answer may be that production is factorable for some kinds of writing and unitary for others, and the writer's task is to know which kind they are doing.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Wang's framework converges with the Tyler-Cowen framing implicit in his own argument: AI as a tool that should arrive in a fully-developed cognitive life and *turbocharge* what is already there, rather than substituting for cognitive infrastructure that hasn't been built yet. The convergence is structural — both Wang and Cowen treat the user's pre-AI cognitive baseline as the input that determines whether AI use produces a multiplier or a substitute. The divergence is in the specific applications: Cowen has been more public about using AI in research and writing in ways Wang would not, suggesting that Cowen's verboten line may sit elsewhere or may not exist at all. The tension reveals that even within the same intellectual circle, the boundary between *consumption-enhancement* and *production-substitution* is drawn differently by different practitioners, and there is no consensus on where the right line is.

A more pointed tension is with the vault's existing AI-collaboration corpus, much of which was built around the assumption that AI can be a creative-production partner if used skillfully. Wang's framework is the strongest articulation in the vault of the *opposite* position: that AI cannot, by structural necessity, be a voice-production partner without degrading voice. The two positions are not equally weighted in the vault as it currently stands, and the addition of Wang's page corrects what may have been an over-weighting of the optimistic AI-as-collaborator framing. The vault now contains both positions and can hold them in productive tension.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The framework reaches into creative practice (the writing-craft implications), psychology (the cognitive mechanism by which sentence-generation produces thought), and cross-domain (the broader question of which cognitive activities are substitutable and which are not).

- **Creative Practice**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/voice-cultivation-through-stylistic-models|Voice Cultivation Through Stylistic Models]] — the verboten rule and the voice-cultivation framework are companion pieces. Voice is built through deliberate exposure to master writers, manuscript copying, and trained intentionality at the sentence level (per the existing voice-cultivation pages). All of that work is *exactly* what the AI sentence-generation would substitute for. The handshake produces a clarifying claim: the AI verboten is not a freestanding stance; it is the necessary conservation of the work that voice-cultivation requires. A writer who follows the voice-cultivation discipline for years and then lets AI produce their sentences is undoing the cumulative result of their training. The two pages should be read as a unit: voice-cultivation is the construction; the verboten is the protection.

- **Eastern Spirituality**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/sadhana-practice-hub|Sadhana Practice Hub]] — the discipline of *not outsourcing the cognitive labor that the practice is for* shows up across spiritual practice traditions. The bhakta who recites mantra cannot delegate the recitation to a recording without losing the practice's effect; the meditator cannot delegate the sitting to an algorithm without losing the meditation; the yogi cannot delegate the asana to a trainer-on-screen without losing the embodied transformation. The handshake reveals: *certain cognitive activities are not factorable.* The transformation produced by the activity is intrinsic to the doing of the activity, and there is no shortcut that preserves the transformation. Wang's writing case is one instance of a much broader principle that operates wherever embodied repetition produces cognitive change. The protection of the practice is the same logic in both cases: the verboten rule for AI in writing is the writing-domain analog of the spiritual injunction against shortcut-substitutes for sadhana.

- **Behavioral-Mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/stage-setting-and-environmental-manipulation|Stage-Setting and Environmental Manipulation]] — the live-before-AI argument is a behavioral-mechanics claim about skill acquisition: the cognitive infrastructure built through pre-AI activity becomes the foundation that AI later multiplies, and skipping the foundation produces a different and lesser cognitive endpoint. The handshake produces an actionable claim for educators and parents: the developmental sequence matters. Children and young adults exposed to AI before they have developed reading, writing, library research, and database fluency may end up with a different cognitive architecture than those who develop the foundational skills first. The difference may not be visible in short-run task performance but may matter enormously for long-run cognitive depth. This is consistent with what teachers and parents anecdotally report and provides a structural framework for why.

- **Cross-Domain**: labor-cognition substitutability (no dedicated vault page yet — flagged as gap; this is a broader epistemological question about which cognitive activities can be automated) — Wang's verboten line is one specific application of a broader epistemological question: which cognitive activities can be substituted by external systems without loss, and which cannot? The mainstream AI-optimist position is that most cognitive activity is substitutable as long as the human provides taste and judgment. The contrary position — to which Wang's framework belongs — holds that some cognitive activities are *constitutive* of the thinker rather than separable products of thought, and substituting them changes who the thinker is rather than merely what they produce. The handshake produces a long-run claim: the resolution of this debate matters not just for individual practice but for how societies structure education, work, and civic life around AI. If the optimist position is right, AI is a productivity multiplier and human cognition continues unchanged; if the verboten position is right, AI use without discipline can hollow out cognitive capacity at scale, and the cumulative effect is invisible until it is too late to reverse.

The four handshakes converge on a single claim: *the boundary between AI-as-multiplier and AI-as-substitute is a real boundary, and where it falls determines whether AI use produces cognitive enrichment or cognitive impoverishment.* The boundary is harder to maintain in practice than in principle, and the discipline of maintaining it — the verboten — is structurally similar to disciplines of practice protection across other domains.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

If voice-bearing writing requires the verboten, then the AI optimist position — that skilled use of AI as creative collaborator can produce voice the way the writer would have on their own — is wrong in a specific way. It is not wrong about the output: AI-assisted writing can produce excellent prose. It is wrong about *what the writer becomes* through the process. The writer who has been letting AI produce sentences for two years does not have the same mind as the writer who has been producing them themselves. The output may look identical from outside; the cognitive endpoint of the writer is different. The implication is uncomfortable for any writer currently using AI in their drafting: even if your output is fine, *you are different than you would have been*, and the difference is not visible to you because the cognition you are not having is exactly the cognition that would have surfaced what you are not seeing. The verboten is therefore not a precaution against bad output; it is a precaution against an invisible degradation that the writer using AI cannot detect from inside the practice. The honest test of whether to maintain the verboten is whether you trust your future self to know what they have lost — and the trouble is that the future self produced by sustained AI-assisted writing may not know.

**Generative Questions**
- The verboten line works for Wang, an established writer with a developed voice. Does it work for early-career writers who have not yet developed voice? Or do they need AI even less, because the cognition AI would substitute for is exactly the cognition they need to be doing?
- What is the equivalent of the verboten in non-writing voice-bearing creative domains? For visual artists, does the same logic apply to AI-generated images used as drafting? For musicians, does it apply to AI-generated melodies used as starting points?
- Wang's line is about *sentences*. Could a writer maintain a partial verboten — *AI may produce structural outlines and research, but not sentences* — and preserve voice while gaining productivity? Or does the partial concession dissolve into full substitution over time as the line drifts?

- The "live half your life without AI" argument depends on Wang's specific cohort (those born around 1990, age 30-35 at ChatGPT's emergence). Does the argument generalize backward to writers who developed under earlier media transitions (typewriter to word processor, paper-mail to email), and forward to writers being trained now under AI?
- Wang explicitly anticipates using AI more for research in his next book (line 410). What is the principled distinction between *AI for research* (allowed) and *AI for sentences* (verboten), and is the line stable, or does it drift over time?

# AI as Tyler Cowen Substitute — Generalist Sparring Partner

## A Tyler-Like Creature in His Pocket

Wang has a friend named Tyler. He sees Tyler maybe once every couple of months — drinks in DC, an afternoon in New York. In between visits, Wang keeps a running list of questions in his notes app: things he is wondering about, half-formed observations he wants Tyler's reaction to, intellectual loose ends. When the next visit comes, Wang shows up and *bombards him with a couple of things that I've been thinking,* and Tyler somehow expects this and absorbs it.[^1]

This Tyler is Tyler Cowen. Economics professor at George Mason. Author of an enormous corpus across economics, food, travel, philosophy, AI, culture. The kind of generalist who can give you a useful reaction to a Beethoven string quartet, a Stendhal novel, a Mongolian noodle, a Catholic theological dispute, a chess opening, and a forecast about the next decade of geopolitics — sometimes in the same conversation. The Tyler-experience for someone like Wang is the experience of having a *generalist sparring partner of unusual depth*, available occasionally, with whom rapid-fire intellectual exchange produces sharper thinking than the person could have produced alone.

Then ChatGPT arrived, and Wang noticed something odd about it.

The voice and the intellectual style of the model felt *familiar*.

## The Tyler-Influence Claim

Wang's claim is specific. *Tyler Cowen's thought has influenced a lot of how ChatGPT communicates*, and *this is on the record, I believe, and this is kind of established.*[^1] The claim refers to the well-known fact that Cowen's writing — across his blog *Marginal Revolution*, his books, his Bloomberg columns, his Conversations with Tyler podcast transcripts — is part of the publicly-available training corpus that LLMs learn on. Cowen has been extraordinarily prolific in public-facing prose for two decades, in a recognizable analytical voice that emphasizes economic reasoning, comparative observation, willingness to hold counterintuitive positions, and a particular kind of rapid-fire associative intelligence. That body of work has been absorbed into the training data of the major LLMs, and the models have learned, among many other things, *how Tyler Cowen thinks*.

The model is not Tyler Cowen. The model is a probabilistic next-token predictor trained on a much larger corpus that includes Cowen alongside millions of other writers. But the *style* of the model's outputs — particularly when prompted on the kinds of questions Cowen would address — has structural fingerprints of Cowen's voice. The model has absorbed the moves: the comparative angle, the unexpected reference, the willingness to take a position quickly, the slight asymmetry between the question being asked and the question the model chooses to answer.

Wang noticed this. And once he noticed it, he started using the model the way he uses Tyler.

## The Substitution Move

The mechanics of the substitution are simple enough to describe but interesting enough to be worth slowing down on.

Wang has built, over years of friendship and mentorship, a *cognitive habit* around Tyler-conversations. He thinks of questions in a particular way because he is anticipating what Tyler would do with them. He keeps the running list. He prepares some context. He shows up ready to spar — to push back, to extend, to reorient the question if Tyler's reaction reveals it was the wrong question.

ChatGPT doesn't have Tyler's actual mind. It has, at best, the Tyler-flavored layer of its training. But for the purposes of Wang's specific cognitive practice — *get a Tyler-like reaction so I can spar with it* — the layer is sufficient. *If I really wanted to have an instant Tyler-like reaction to a novel that I've just read or a piece of music that I've just heard, I just ask ChatGPT, and it is able to give me some really good answers.*[^1] The model produces a reaction that triggers the same mental sparring move Wang would have made with Tyler in person. Wang's cognition continues from there: he pushes back, extends, adjusts. The model, like Tyler in person, gives him something to *think against*.

The substitution is incomplete in important ways. Tyler-the-person remembers earlier conversations; the model does not (within a session) and even with memory features cannot reconstruct the depth of accumulated context Tyler has on Wang specifically. Tyler-the-person can introduce Wang to other people, push him into specific writing opportunities, model intellectual virtues over a multi-year arc. The model does none of this. The substitution captures one particular feature of Tyler — *generalist sparring reactions in real-time* — and substitutes a much weaker version of Tyler in all the other dimensions, mostly absent.

But for the use case Wang is describing — *I just read Stendhal, I want a smart reaction so my own thinking can sharpen against it; I just heard Mahler, I want a musicological gloss so I can extend my own reaction* — the substitution works. The model is not Tyler. It is a *Tyler-like creature*, available at any time, infinitely patient, free at the margin. Wang treats it as such.

## The Spanish Inquisition Question

The example Wang gives of his first really good ChatGPT experience is a small one but it captures the texture of the practice.

*Why did the Spanish Catholic Church develop such a virulent inquisition whereas the Austrian Catholics had no inquisition?*[^1]

The question itself is the kind Wang would have asked Tyler. It is comparative. It pulls together two things normally treated separately (Spanish Catholicism, Austrian Catholicism) and asks for a structural account of their divergence. It is not a question with a quick Wikipedia answer; it requires synthesizing across history, theology, political economy, ethnology. It is a question whose value is partly in *the texture of a good answer* — what considerations the answerer brings forward, which factors they weight, what comparative cases they invoke.

Wang has the question because he has spent time in both Catholic worlds and felt the difference. *Spanish Catholicism feels gloomy and slightly violent and a little bit dark; Austrian Catholicism feels bright, joyful, resplendent, much more crimson rather than very black.*[^1] The question is not abstract. It has been generated by Wang's own observational experience of two religious cultures and the felt-sense that the difference must be explainable.

He asked the model. The model produced an answer that *felt right*.[^1] We do not get the answer in the transcript — the relevant point is not what the model said but that the conversation succeeded as the kind of intellectual exchange Wang had previously been having with Tyler. The model produced a structural account that addressed the question on its own terms, mobilized appropriate comparative material, and gave Wang something to push against.

The Spanish-vs-Austrian question is the canonical instance of what the AI-as-Tyler-substitute can do well. Comparative, structural, requiring generalist synthesis, not requiring deep specialist accuracy. The model excels at exactly this register. It is less reliable on questions that require precise factual recall (where hallucinations bite) or on questions that require deep specialist judgment (where the model averages across sources rather than reasoning from expertise). The Tyler-substitute use case is in the *middle layer* — questions that benefit from broad intellectual range and structural thinking, without requiring expertise that exceeds what the model can plausibly synthesize.

## The Sparring Architecture

Perell's framing of what Wang is describing is worth dwelling on. Most users approach AI by asking it for *answers*. Wang approaches AI by asking it for *reactions to push against*. The reframing changes the cognitive role of the AI.

In the answer-mode, the AI's output is the destination. The user receives the output, accepts or rejects it, moves on. The user's cognitive activity is filtering rather than producing.

In the sparring-mode, the AI's output is the *instigator*. The user has a half-formed question or hypothesis. The AI produces a response that triggers the user's own cognitive engagement — agreement that extends the thinking, disagreement that sharpens it, partial acceptance that splits the question into newer questions. The user's cognitive activity is producing rather than filtering.

The sparring architecture is what Wang has imported from his Tyler-relationship into his AI use. *That's the process of thinking through things. That's the process of trying to figure out what are the right questions and what is the right approach, what is the right observational style.*[^1] The AI is not telling Wang what to think. It is providing a *worthy interlocutor* whose responses are good enough that Wang's own thinking is sharpened by reacting to them.

The architecture has a subtle prerequisite. The user has to already *have* something to spar with. The hypothesis, the half-formed observation, the question generated by their own engagement with material the AI has not seen. Without that input, the user is just asking the AI for an answer, and the AI produces an answer, and the cognitive engagement is the answer-mode rather than the sparring-mode. The sparring requires the user to *bring something* to the conversation, and the more interesting the user brings, the more useful the model's reaction becomes.

## What This Implies for AI Practice

The Tyler-substitute framework converts cleanly into a practice principle. *Use AI for the generalist-reaction function, in conversations you initiate with material you have already engaged with.* The good prompts in this register are not *teach me X* but *I have been thinking about X, and here is what I noticed, what would you say back?* The model becomes useful not as an oracle but as an interlocutor. The user's pre-existing engagement is what the model's reaction can sharpen.

The framework also implies that AI use has a *generalist substitute layer* and a *specialist substitute layer*, and they should be evaluated differently. For generalist sparring (comparative history, music, art, philosophy, structural analysis), the model is genuinely useful and the Tyler-substitute mode applies. For specialist work (technical implementation, primary-source research, expert judgment in domains where the model averages across mediocre sources), the model is much less useful and the user should not be using it the same way. Confusing the two layers — using the model for specialist work in the generalist mode — is where the hallucination problems and the bad-citation problems concentrate.

## Evidence

[^1] Wang's account of the Tyler-substitute use of AI runs from lines 444-462 of the transcript. Specific claims and locations: "Tyler Cowan thought has influenced a lot of how ChatGPT communicates" + "on the record, kind of established" (line 446); "the way that I treat ChatGPT is as my friend Tyler, who I maybe see once every couple of months in DC or in New York" (line 448); "instant Tyler-like reaction to a novel that I've just read or a piece of music that I've just heard" (line 450); running list of questions for Tyler in notes (line 452); Spanish vs Austrian Catholic Inquisition question + Spanish "gloomy slightly violent dark" vs Austrian "bright joyful resplendent crimson" + first really good ChatGPT experience (lines 456-460); "Tyler-like creature in my pocket" (line 460); "process of thinking through things... finding the right questions, right approach, right observational style" (line 462); reaffirmation of the verboten on flat sentences in writing (line 462).

## Tensions

The framework has tensions with both the AI-skeptic and AI-optimist positions.

Against the *AI-skeptic* position that LLMs cannot produce useful intellectual exchange because they are stochastic parrots without understanding, Wang's framework offers a counter-example. The Tyler-substitute use of AI is, by Wang's account, genuinely cognitively productive — it produces the same kind of thinking-sharpening that human conversation with a generalist intellectual produces. The skeptic position has to either dismiss Wang's experience as illusion or concede that, at the level of cognitive function rather than ontology, the model is doing something useful regardless of whether it "understands."

Against the *AI-optimist* position that LLMs can replace human intellectual exchange entirely, Wang's framework also offers a check. The Tyler-substitute is *for specific use cases* — generalist sparring on material the user has already engaged with. The model is *not* a substitute for the long-arc relationship Wang has with Tyler-the-person, for the deep specialist work Wang does on China, or for the writing that constitutes Wang's voice. The optimist position has to recognize that the AI-as-intellectual-companion role is genuine but bounded.

The harder tension is over the *Tyler-influence* claim itself. The empirical fact that Cowen's writing has influenced ChatGPT is plausible (Cowen is widely read and represented in training corpora) but also somewhat anecdotal and unverified at the precise level Wang is claiming. The vault should hold this as Wang's reading rather than as an empirical fact, and remain open to the possibility that the *Tyler-flavor* Wang detects is partly a function of Wang's expectations and partly a function of the model's training rather than a clean attribution.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The framework converges with Wang's own [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/ai-as-consumption-enhancer-not-writing-tool|AI as Consumption Enhancer, Not Writing Tool]] page (the companion concept). Both pages are products of Wang's overall AI framework: AI is excellent at the *layer wrapped around the user's experience* (consumption-enhancement, generalist-sparring) and verboten at the *layer that constitutes the user's cognitive output* (sentence-generation, voice). The two pages should be read together as the two sides of Wang's framework.

The framework also tensions with the broader AI-collaboration corpus in the vault. [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/beta-editor-review-skill|Beta Editor Review Skill]] and adjacent pages treat AI as a simulated audience or wind-tunnel for testing one's own ideas. Wang's Tyler-substitute framing is similar but more specific — the AI is not a generic audience but a specifically-flavored interlocutor whose particular intellectual disposition (generalist, comparative, willing to take a position) makes it useful in a way a generic-audience framing does not capture. The convergence is on the underlying claim that AI is a thinking-partner; the divergence is in how specifically the partner can be characterized. Wang's framing implies that AI-as-thinking-partner is most useful when the user has a specific, characterized interlocutor model in mind, not when they are using the AI as a generic foil.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The Tyler-substitute framework reaches into psychology (the cognitive function of having a sparring partner), creative practice (the role of intellectual exchange in producing original work), and behavioral mechanics (the specific architecture of what makes a conversation productive).

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/identity-architecture-and-defense-hub|Identity Architecture and Defense Hub]] — the importance of *trusted interlocutors* in the development of mature thinking is well-documented in developmental psychology. Adolescents and young adults develop intellectual identity partly through extended sparring with a few mentors whose perspectives they argue with, internalize, and eventually push beyond. The handshake reveals that AI-as-Tyler-substitute is operating in the same psychological space — the user is engaging with a characterized interlocutor whose responses sharpen their own thinking — but with two important differences: the interlocutor is not real (which may matter for identity formation in ways the framework does not address) and the interlocutor is infinitely patient (which removes the social stakes that sometimes make human sparring more cognitively engaging). The implication: AI-substitute interlocutors may be useful for thinking-sharpening but may be inadequate substitutes for human mentors in identity-formation work, and the user should know which function they are using AI for.

- **Creative Practice**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/voice-cultivation-through-stylistic-models|Voice Cultivation Through Stylistic Models]] — the Tyler-substitute is, in a sense, a way of importing Cowen's stylistic intuitions into the user's own thinking process via the AI's training-influenced outputs. The handshake reveals a non-obvious symmetry: the writer who deliberately copies New Yorker articles and the user who deliberately uses ChatGPT-as-Tyler-substitute are doing structurally similar things — exposing themselves to a particular intellectual style in order to absorb its operations into their own thinking. The difference is the medium (handwritten/typed reproduction vs. AI conversation) and the granularity (sentence-level for copying, prompt-response-level for AI). Both are *deliberate exposure to a style* with the goal of cognitive transformation. Both are subject to the same caveat: choose your sources strategically, because the style you absorb shapes the thinking you become capable of.

- **Behavioral-Mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/behavioral-mechanics-hub|Behavioral Mechanics Hub]] (specifically pages on questioning techniques and elicitation) — the sparring architecture Wang describes is structurally similar to behavioral-mechanics protocols for generative questioning. The questioner brings specific material; the responder produces a reaction; the questioner pushes back; the productive thinking happens in the back-and-forth rather than in either side's individual contribution. The handshake produces an actionable claim: users who want to extract maximum value from AI conversation should approach it as a behavioral-mechanics protocol — bring specific input, ask for specific reactions rather than open-ended assistance, push back on the AI's responses rather than accepting them, iterate until the conversation produces something the user could not have produced alone. This is a learnable skill, not a default behavior, and most AI users are not yet practicing it.

- **Eastern Spirituality**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/sadhana-practice-hub|Sadhana Practice Hub]] — the running-list-of-questions practice Wang describes (questions for Tyler accumulated in his notes app, then unloaded when they meet) has a structural cousin in the spiritual practice of *holding questions for the next encounter with one's teacher*. In both cases, the questioner accumulates questions over time, lets them ripen, and presents them when the encounter happens. The handshake reveals that the practice is not about the immediate availability of the answer; it is about the *discipline of articulating the question well enough that it survives the wait*. The questions that survive accumulation and articulation tend to be better questions than the questions that get asked impulsively in the moment of confusion. The implication for AI use: even though the AI is always available, users may benefit from imposing artificial accumulation — keep questions for the AI in a running list, let them ripen, ask in batches rather than as they arrive — because the discipline produces better questions and better cognitive value from the eventual conversations.

The four handshakes converge on a single claim: *AI-as-sparring-partner is one specific application of a much broader principle about how thinking is sharpened through structured exchange with a characterized interlocutor*, and the value of the practice depends on the user's discipline in bringing material, characterizing the interlocutor, and treating the exchange as iterative rather than transactional.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

If the Tyler-substitute framework is correct, then the public conversation about AI's intellectual role is operating at the wrong level of generality. The question is not *can AI replace human intellectual exchange* (the answer is partly yes, partly no, depending on which functions of intellectual exchange you mean). The question is *which specific intellectual functions can which specific kinds of AI substitute for, and how much of the user's existing cognitive infrastructure does each substitution require*. Wang's case shows that AI can substitute for a specific friend's specific function (generalist sparring on material Wang has engaged with) for a user with specific cognitive infrastructure (an analytical writer with a pre-existing relationship to the friend). The substitution does not generalize: AI cannot substitute for the friend's other functions (mentorship, introductions, identity-formation) and cannot substitute for any function for users who lack the relevant cognitive infrastructure. The implication for AI policy and pedagogy is that the right questions are *narrow and specific*, not *broad and abstract*. Public conversation that treats AI's intellectual role as a single thing — *AI is good for thinking* or *AI cannot really think* — is missing the actual differentiation that determines whether any specific use produces cognitive enrichment or impoverishment.

**Generative Questions**
- Could a user deliberately *cultivate* AI-substitute relationships for multiple specific intellectual styles? Wang has Tyler. Could the same user develop their AI use to substitute for Cowen-on-economics, Hitchens-on-rhetoric, Eliot-on-poetry, and so on, by recognizing the trained-in stylistic fingerprints of different authors and prompting accordingly?
- Wang's running-list practice was developed for human friends and ported to AI. Are there other human-relationship cognitive practices that would port well to AI use, and which ones port badly?
- The *Tyler-influence* claim is interesting because it implies AI's outputs are *characterized* in ways most users may not recognize. If trained-in stylistic fingerprints are real, are users systematically being shaped by the styles their AI-of-choice reflects, in ways that average toward whichever writers are most heavily represented in training corpora? Is there a quiet homogenization happening at scale?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/ai-as-consumption-enhancer-not-writing-tool|AI as Consumption Enhancer, Not Writing Tool]] — companion concept; Wang's framework's other side
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/beta-editor-review-skill|Beta Editor Review Skill]] — adjacent AI-as-interlocutor framing
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/voice-cultivation-through-stylistic-models|Voice Cultivation Through Stylistic Models]] — structural cousin in the creative-practice domain
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/manuscript-copying-as-voice-training|Manuscript Copying as Voice Training]] — embodied analog of the same exposure mechanism
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/transformer-architecture-and-language-model-mechanics|Transformer Architecture and Language Model Mechanics]] — the technical layer that explains why training-corpus stylistic fingerprints exist

## Open Questions

- What is the actual evidence for the Cowen-influence-on-ChatGPT claim? Is this established in any documentable way, or is it widely-asserted-but-unverified? Wang treats it as common knowledge but the original citation is unclear.
- The Tyler-substitute framework requires the user to already have a relationship with a Tyler. Is the framework usable by users who don't have a Tyler — and if so, can they characterize the AI's interlocutor role through other means (specifying author personas in prompts, etc.)?
- Wang sees Tyler in person every few months. As AI conversation becomes default, does the value of in-person Tyler-equivalent relationships rise or fall? Are people who have access to both AI substitutes and human intellectual mentors at an advantage that compounds, or does AI substitution erode the human relationships over time?

## Cross-Source: Karlsson — AI as Targeted-Craft-Tool, Not Interlocutor (2026-05-12)

Henrik Karlsson adds a third position to this page's framing of AI use, structurally distinct from Wang's two frames (Cowen-substitute sparring partner; consumption-enhancer for reading). Karlsson uses AI for *targeted craft-mechanical tasks* — vocabulary lookup, grammar verification, sentence-variation generation, and bad-habits monitoring — comprising about 1% of his published words.[^2]

The four micro-uses Karlsson articulates:

**1. Lexical lookup for second-language gaps.** As a non-native English speaker, Karlsson uses the model as a thesaurus-on-demand: describe the meaning, get the candidate word. *"I might do things like — because I'm a second language, I don't know English all that well. Sometimes I'll describe a word and they'll give me the word because I don't know it."*[^2]

**2. Grammar verification.** Sanity-check on uncertain constructions. *"Or I'll ask, 'Is this grammatical?' or whatever."*[^2]

**3. Sentence-variation generation.** When stuck on a phrasing: *"Sometimes I'm not happy with a way something is phrased and I'll be like, 'Give me 10 versions of this with different words to just get me out of my head and see different possibilities.'"*[^2] The model is not asked to pick a version — it's asked to display a range, which the writer then selects from or uses as a launchpad.

**4. Bad-habits monitoring.** Karlsson stores his known writing-flaws in a prompt and has the model flag them during edit. *"I have a prompt where I ask it to go through, 'These are some words I overuse, can you point out when I use them?' These are other things I want to think about, just to help it remind me so I don't have to keep all the things I should look out for in my head."*[^2] The model offloads vigilance.

The Karlsson framing differs from Wang's Cowen-substitute frame in a structural way. Wang uses AI as *interlocutor* — conversational partner for thinking-through-problems, with characterized intellectual style influencing the exchange. Karlsson uses AI as *tool* — discrete craft-mechanical tasks with no expectation of intellectual exchange. The model is not Karlsson's thinking partner; it's his lookup, his variation engine, his vigilance store.

Karlsson is also a *power user* of LLMs — pre-ChatGPT access (special OpenAI beta from 2021), deep technical familiarity. His position is not knee-jerk avoidance. He's enthusiastic about the technology while specifically routing around it for substantive writing-work. *"I've been somewhat underwhelmed in what they've delivered so far. I've seen interesting images, interesting music, but I've not yet seen any good literature be made. They are incredible tools for research."*[^2]

The third-position-frame this opens: AI can be used at multiple resolutions of *substance*, and the appropriate use depends on the user's writing-practice.

- **Wang #1 (Cowen-substitute / interlocutor)**: AI for thinking-with at conversational scale. Useful for analytical writers who want characterized sparring partners.
- **Wang #2 (consumption-enhancer / reading tool)**: AI for ingesting and processing source material. Useful for writers in research-intensive practices.
- **Karlsson #3 (targeted-craft-tool / micro-mechanic)**: AI for discrete word/grammar/variation/edit tasks. Useful for writers whose substantive work happens outside the tool.

Karlsson also articulates a deeper concern this page hasn't addressed: **LLMs as standardization-pressure on the prose-field**. He argues that even non-LLM-using writers face ambient smoothing-pressure as LLM-edited text circulates more widely. The defense, in his framing, is to be *wilder with grammar* — deliberately import constructions from other languages (Turkish, Persian, Swedish) to maintain distance from the statistical center the models pull toward. *"LLMs are just another force for standardization. If English is poised to become the global language, we should make an effort to bring in all the weird innovations from all the other languages."*[^2] This is a structural-ecology claim, not a personal-use claim — and it adds a layer to the business framework neither Wang frame addresses.

The full three-frame picture: Wang's two frames optimize for *what AI does well* (interlocutor; consumption-helper); Karlsson's frame optimizes for *minimal AI presence in production* combined with *defensive practice against ambient standardization*. All three positions are coherent. They suit different writers and different writing-philosophies. The implication for this page: AI-as-Cowen-substitute is one of *several legitimate counter-positions* to mainstream AI-as-creative-collaborator framing, and the full counter-framework needs all three to be complete.

See [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/llm-as-standardization-pressure-grammar-wildness-defense|LLM as Standardization Pressure — Grammar Wildness as Defense]] for the full Karlsson treatment.

# Attitude vs Aptitude — Hire for Lowest Skill Deficiency

## The Hiring Heuristic That Reframes The Whole Question

The folk wisdom: *"Hire for attitude, train for aptitude."* It's been printed on enough HR posters to feel obvious. But Hormozi argues it's an unhelpful slogan because "attitude" is a bundle of many underlying skills, and the right hiring frame is more precise.[^1]

The Hormozi reframe: *hire for the lowest skill deficiency.* What that means: identify what skills are deficient in the candidate, calculate the cost of training each, and hire the candidate whose deficiencies are cheapest to train. The variable being optimized is *training-cost-to-effectiveness ratio*, not "attitude" or "aptitude" abstractly.

This sounds technical but it's actually clarifying. When you bundle 20 underlying skills under the word "kindness," you can't tell whether a candidate is teachable in those skills. When you unbundle the bundle and ask "which specific deficiencies does this candidate have, and what would it cost to train each?", you can make an actual hiring decision.

## What This Actually Is

A hiring framework with three operating components:

1. **Unbundle the bundled terms.** "Hardworking" isn't a skill — it's a shorthand for ~20 underlying behaviors. List them explicitly. "Charismatic" isn't a skill either — it's a shorthand for tonality, eye contact, conviction-projection, conversational pacing, and humor. List those.

2. **Identify which deficiencies are present in the candidate.** For each underlying behavior, is the candidate already proficient, or do they need training?

3. **Calculate training cost per deficiency.** Some skills (reading a script, calling leads, BAMFAM) train in 2-3 weeks. Others (developing genuine warmth, sustaining conviction through resistance, reading interpersonal dynamics) train in months-to-years or not at all. The cost-of-training varies wildly.

4. **Hire the candidate whose deficiencies are cheapest to train.** A candidate who lacks script-knowledge but has natural warmth is cheaper to train than a candidate who knows the script but lacks warmth. Train the script; you can't train warmth.

## Why The Folk Wisdom Was Half-Right

The classical "hire for attitude" rule works because *some* of the bundled traits (kindness, warmth, conviction) are genuinely hard to train. So if you're choosing between a kind person who doesn't know the script and an unkind person who knows it, hiring the kind person is correct — but not because attitude beats aptitude as a general rule. Because in *this specific tradeoff*, the kindness-training-cost exceeds the script-training-cost.

The reverse case exists. A candidate with deep technical knowledge in a specific niche (transactional CFO, 50-deal M&A experience) is genuinely scarce. In that case, the underlying-skills tradeoff flips: training a kind-but-unqualified candidate to be a transactional CFO might be impossible, while training a transactional CFO to behave better culturally might be feasible.[^2]

The rule isn't "hire for attitude always." It's: *hire for the lowest skill deficiency*, which depends on what skills are scarce and what skills are cheap to train *in the specific role you're hiring for.*

## The Levels Where The Rule Flips

The rule's calibration depends on the role's seniority:

- **Junior/entry-level roles** (setters, junior closers, customer-success reps): bundled-behavior deficiencies (kindness, conviction, hustle) are more expensive to train than role-specific skills (script-adherence, CRM-usage, ticket-resolution). Hire on temperament.

- **Senior/expert roles** (senior closers, sales directors, technical specialists): specialized skill deficiencies (industry knowledge, technical expertise, scarce credentials) are more expensive to acquire than cultural-fit behaviors. Hire on specialized capability and train cultural fit.

The classical "hire for attitude" is right for junior roles and wrong for senior roles. The Hormozi reframe captures both cases under one principle: *the lowest-training-cost deficiency wins.*[^3]

## Synergies & Handshakes

This principle composes with:
- **Dogs, horses, tigers** — temperament is one of the bundled traits that's expensive to train (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/dogs-horses-tigers-three-salesperson-archetypes|Dogs, Horses, Tigers]]).
- **Group interview vs resume screening** — group interviews surface bundled-behavior signals; resumes surface specialized-skill signals. Use the method that matches the role's seniority (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/group-interview-vs-resume-screening|Group Interview vs Resume Screening]]).
- **Sales director — hire one to hire ten first** — the senior-role case study where specialized-skill matters most (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/sales-director-hire-one-to-hire-ten-first|Sales Director — Hire One to Hire Ten First]]).
- **Compensation attracts ≠ retains** — comp design follows the same logic: comp brings candidates in; the trainable-deficiency reality determines whether they succeed (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/compensation-attracts-doesnt-retain|Compensation Attracts ≠ Retains]]).
- **Daily huddle roleplay** — the training architecture that determines what's actually trainable (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/daily-huddle-roleplay-with-fast-feedback-loop|Daily Huddle Roleplay]]).

## Analytical Case Study: The Mortgage-Rep With Eroded Conviction

Returning to the John-the-mortgage-rep case (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/conviction-corrects-tone-trick-vs-train|Conviction Corrects Tone]] and [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/sales-as-transference-of-belief-over-bridge-of-trust|Sales as Transference of Belief]]): John knew the script. His scripted-skill deficiency was near zero. But his conviction was missing — and conviction is expensive to train if the underlying belief-substrate is wrong.

The hiring lens: had the company been hiring on the right deficiency-stack, they might have realized that conviction-capacity (the ability to believe in something deeply and project it) was the deficiency they couldn't easily fix. Script-skill was cheap. Conviction was expensive. The hire failed not because John was a bad person but because the deficiency-cost calculation was wrong at hire time.

The case shows the diagnostic value of the framework. When a closer fails operationally, you can ask: *which underlying deficiency was the binding constraint?* Then you adjust hiring criteria to surface that deficiency at interview-time for the next hire.

## Implementation Workflow

You're hiring for a new junior closer role. You have three candidates after the group interview:

**Candidate A**: 5 years of mortgage-industry sales experience. Clear knowledge of the relevant scripts. Warmth seems thin in interview. Conviction in our product unclear.

**Candidate B**: No industry experience. Career-change candidate from teaching. Visible warmth in group interview. Asked deep questions about our customer-outcomes. Seems genuinely curious about the work.

**Candidate C**: 2 years of B2C sales in unrelated category. Mixed warmth. Strong on script-knowledge. Doesn't seem to care deeply about our specific product.

You unbundle the deficiencies:

- **Script knowledge**: cheap to train (2-3 weeks of huddles).
- **Industry-specific patterns**: moderate to train (2-3 months of exposure).
- **Genuine warmth toward customers**: expensive to train (months to years; sometimes not trainable).
- **Conviction in our specific product**: moderately expensive (requires testimonial exposure, customer-success ride-alongs, founder narrative).

Candidate A: deficient in warmth and conviction. Both expensive.
Candidate B: deficient in script and industry patterns. Both cheap-to-moderate.
Candidate C: deficient in warmth and conviction. Both expensive.

You hire Candidate B. The folk-wisdom version ("hire for attitude") would have produced the same answer, but the framework gives you a defensible reason. Three months later, Candidate B is performing at team-average. Six months later, above-average. The training investment paid back.

You also document the lesson for the next hire: *the deficiencies we can train fastest are script and industry. The deficiencies we can't easily train are warmth and conviction. Hire on the un-trainable variables.*

## The Attitude-vs-Aptitude Failure (Diagnostic Signs)

- **You're hiring on industry experience for entry-level roles.** The wrong calibration. Industry experience is cheap to train at entry-level; you're optimizing for the wrong variable.
- **You're hiring on culture-fit for senior specialist roles.** The wrong calibration. Specialized expertise is what you can't train at senior level; culture-fit is the cheap variable.
- **You can't articulate the specific deficiencies of any candidate.** You're hiring on gestalt impression rather than analytical decomposition. The hires will be inconsistent.
- **You hired on attitude and the person can't learn the basics in 6 months.** Either the basics aren't trainable in 6 months (revisit assumption), or you mis-measured attitude (revisit interview process).
- **You hired on specialized-skill and the person damages culture immediately.** You optimized the wrong variable for this role. Adjust the hiring framework for the next hire.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The hire-for-lowest-skill-deficiency framework and the classical hiring tradition (Drucker, Buckingham, Topgrading, the Smart-Topgrading methodology) converge on the analytical decomposition of "good hire" but vary on emphasis.

Topgrading (Brad Smart) explicitly decomposes hiring into specific competencies and trains hiring managers to assess each. The framework is congruent with Hormozi's unbundling — both reject the use of vague terms like "attitude" without underlying behavioral specificity.

The divergence: Hormozi adds the *training-cost calculation* layer that Topgrading doesn't emphasize. Topgrading helps you identify which competencies a candidate has; Hormozi adds: now compute training-cost per missing competency and optimize for the lowest total.

The convergence with the strengths-based tradition (Buckingham): both agree that hiring is about identifying alignment between candidate-strengths and role-requirements. The divergence: Hormozi's framework is more operations-focused (training-cost is the explicit variable), while Buckingham is more developmental (long-run strengths-fit is the variable).

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The hire-for-lowest-skill-deficiency framework isn't just a sales-team tactic. It's a resource-allocation discipline that shows up in any operator-selection context.

- **Behavioral Mechanics**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/hubs/manipulation-and-influence-hub|Manipulation and Influence Hub]] — every domain that selects operators for influence work (sales, politics, military operations, diplomacy) faces the same hiring challenge: which deficiencies are trainable and which aren't? Hughes's behavioral-cluster work implicitly assumes operators are trainable on the clusters, but the underlying temperament (intrinsic warmth, comfort with ambiguity, conviction-capacity) is often what determines who can deploy the clusters effectively. The structural parallel: every influence-work selection context faces the same trainable-vs-untrainable decomposition. The insight: the Hormozi framework is a meta-principle for operator-selection in any influence-work domain. The specific deficiency-stack varies by domain; the framework is invariant.

- **Eastern Spirituality**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/sadhana-as-staged-practice-architecture|Sadhana as Staged Practice Architecture]] — traditional guru-disciple selection processes evaluate practitioners on what's called *adhikara* (capacity for the practice), which is essentially a deficiency-trainability assessment. Some practitioners lack scriptural knowledge but have deep sincerity (trainable on scripture, hard to train on sincerity); others have scriptural knowledge but lack sincerity (the inverse, often considered harder to develop into genuine practice). The structural parallel: traditional spiritual lineages have run the trainable-vs-untrainable analysis for millennia. The insight: every operator-selection context — sales, spiritual practice, medicine, education — eventually develops some version of the framework. The Hormozi version is operationally crisp; the spiritual-tradition versions are richer in identifying which qualities are genuinely deep-rooted vs. surface-trainable.

- **Business**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/dogs-horses-tigers-three-salesperson-archetypes|Dogs, Horses, Tigers]] — the temperament taxonomy maps onto the trainability question. Tigers have low deficiency in intrinsic-drive (the most expensive trait to train); horses have moderate deficiency; dogs have high deficiency. Hiring on the dog-horse-tiger spectrum is the same exercise as hiring on lowest-skill-deficiency, just framed differently. The structural parallel: temperament-classification and skill-deficiency-classification are two angles on the same hiring decision. The insight: the underlying variable both frameworks are tracking is *which traits are deep enough to require selection at hiring rather than training post-hire.*

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

The hire-for-lowest-skill-deficiency framework implies that *most hiring decisions are made on the wrong variable.* Companies that hire on "good fit" or "right attitude" or "strong resume" are using shorthand for an underlying trainable-vs-untrainable analysis they're not running explicitly. When they do run it explicitly, the hiring decisions become more consistent and the team's training-investment ROI improves. The framework requires more upfront thinking — identifying specific deficiencies and computing training costs — but the cost is one-time-per-role-design while the benefit compounds across every hire.

The deeper implication: hiring is *not* a generic process. The right deficiencies to filter for vary by role's seniority, by training-architecture maturity, and by the specific competitive landscape (what skills are scarce in the market). Operations that develop role-specific deficiency frameworks outperform operations that use generic hiring playbooks.

**Generative Questions**

- How do you train hiring managers to run the deficiency-decomposition analysis without it becoming overly mechanical? Probably with structured templates per role-type that decompose "attitude" and "aptitude" into specific behaviors with training-cost estimates. The template makes the analysis routine without forcing the manager to reason from scratch each time.

- Is there a domain where the framework fails? Probably very-low-volume executive hiring where the candidate pool is so small that you're not optimizing-among-options but choosing-or-not-choosing one candidate. There, the framework collapses into a yes/no fit check rather than a comparative analysis.

- How do training-cost estimates stay current as the team's training architecture matures? Probably through after-action-review on hires every 90 days. If you hired Candidate B six months ago expecting them to take 3 months to baseline and they're actually taking 6, your training-cost estimate was off. Update the framework for the next hire.
